disparage

dih-SPAIR-ij · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To disparage is to speak of someone or something in a way that suggests they are unimportant or of little value.

The senior partner would routinely disparage junior associates' work in front of clients, calling their research 'amateurish' even when it was accurate.

Example

Rather than offering useful feedback, the food reviewer disparaged the entire menu as amateur cooking dressed up with expensive plating.

To disparage something is to actively talk it down -- not just disagree with it, but present it as worthless or embarrassing.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

belittle: To belittle is to make someone or their work seem smaller than it is -- often with a dismissive wave, a smirk, or a single cutting word. To disparage is always done in words: you speak of the work as if it had little value. Belittling can be wordless; disparaging never is.

mock: To mock is to make fun of something in a scornful way -- imitating it, joking at its expense, inviting others to laugh. To disparage needs no jokes at all: a flat, serious dismissal of something's value counts, however politely it is delivered.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

praise: to express approval or admiration

commend: to praise formally

Where it sits · how much contempt the comments carry — criticize → disparage → scorn

criticize vs. disparage: To criticize is just to point out flaws -- it doesn't necessarily belittle someone the way disparaging them does.

scorn vs. disparage: Scorn goes further than disparage, showing open contempt rather than just talking something down.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — dis-

prefix — dis-: apart, away, not (Latin dis-)

root — -parage

root — -parage: equal rank (from Latin par, 'equal') (Old French parage)

Put it together

Put it together: Disparage comes from dis- ('apart, away') plus an old root meaning 'equal rank,' from Latin par ('equal'). To disparage someone originally meant to match them unequally -- to treat them as less than equal -- which is exactly what disparaging someone still does today: it talks them down.

Use the root in a new word: disparity

Use the root in a new word: disparity: A disparity is a noticeable gap or difference between things that should otherwise be equal -- from the same par ('equal') root as disparage.

Root Check

Word Choice

Disparage always targets something specific -- a person's work, an idea, a plan -- rather than describing a general mood; you disparage a thing, not just feel grumpy.
